signType: Settlement sign III-14 'Naselje' (yellow, black frame, start of settlement rules). The same yellow sign without a frame only names a dispersed settlement and does not set 50 km/h. Its number (III-14.1) was not confirmed
border: none: a narrow yellow rim runs outside the black frame (rim ~1.5-2% of height, approximate)
innerBorder: black #1E1E1E, ~2.5% of height, inset ~1.5-2%, rounded. Proportions are borrowed from the German sign, because the Slovenian dimensions were not found
lettering: SNV, according to Wikipedia; some signs mix in Arial or Helvetica (sources disagree). The Pravilnik says text is lowercase unless a sign says otherwise, so names appear in mixed case, e.g. 'Bled'. Free alternative: Barlow Semi Condensed Medium or Roboto Condensed. Black
extras: Confirmed: the Pravilnik uses a yellow base with black text and symbols for all roads except motorways and expressways, so direction signs are black on yellow as well. Confirmed: the frame means settlement rules (50 km/h) apply, and the borderless sign keeps the previous limit. Wikipedia's claim that 'yellow means roadworks' is about warning signs, not these. Motorways are white on green and expressways white on blue (one guide disagrees). The yellow hex is a RAL 1023 approximation from W3Schools; other conversions range from #F7B500 to #FAD201, and no RAL value appears in the Slovenian rules found
wear: Two galvanised round steel posts. Retroreflective yellow is slightly faded, with road dirt at the lower edge. Rural verge

signType: Town-entry sign 'Ortstafel' (StVO §53 Abs. 1 Z. 17a)
border: blue #0E518D (RAL 5017 approximation from W3Schools; other conversions are #005B8C and #006793; no official RAL was found). The band runs to the sign edge, ~7-8% of height. Its width and whether it reaches the edge were NOT confirmed by a source
innerBorder: none (the white field sits directly inside the blue band)
lettering: Tern: tested from 2010 and mandatory for new signs since 3 Oct 2013 (BGBl. II 292/2013). Many older signs still use 'Austria', a modified DIN 1451. Tern is not free; close free alternatives are Fira Sans Condensed SemiBold or Source Sans 3 SemiBold. Black, mixed case
cornerRadius: slightly rounded, ~3-4% of height (approximate, not sourced)
extras: Confirmed: a light (white) field with a blue frame and dark text since 1 Jan 1977. Before that the signs had blue bars at the top and bottom, which went out after a 10-year transition. Ortsende (Z. 17b) is the same design with a red diagonal bar. Bilingual signs exist in Carinthia and Burgenland; Oberwart and Oberpullendorf are the only bilingual district capitals. The white is RAL 9016 (approximate). Do not put a district line under the name: sources only confirm it on historic 'Ortschaftstafeln'
wear: Aluminium panel on galvanised posts, clean and reflective. Grit at the lower edge. Snow poles often stand nearby

signType: Town-entry sign 'Ortstafel', Zeichen 310 (StVO Anlage 3)
border: none: a narrow yellow rim ('Lichtkante', 10 mm on a 600 mm-high sign, ~1.7% of height) runs outside the black frame
innerBorder: black #1E1E1E, ~2.5% of height (15 mm 'Randbreite' on a 600 mm-high sign), inset ~1.7%, rounded corners. These figures are from the StVO 1992 drawing of Zeichen 311-50; the researcher's 3% was slightly too wide
lettering: DIN 1451 Mittelschrift (Engschrift for long names). Free alternative: D-DIN (OFL). Black, mixed case
extras: Black text in a black frame on yellow. The yellow is RAL 1023 traffic yellow; hex conversions disagree (#F0CA00 W3Schools, #F7B500 Pontata, #F9BA09 Hextoral, #FAD201 elsewhere), so pick one of these. A smaller second line with the municipality or district is common. The back is Zeichen 311, with the town name crossed out in red and the next place below. Bundesstrasse direction signs are black on yellow, and Autobahn signs are white on blue
wear: Two grey galvanised posts. Reflective, fairly clean, light road grime at the bottom

signType: Direction sign F29 (white on blue), per the Ministerial Decree of 11 Oct 1976 and AWV Order 2018/4. Town-entry F1a/F1b is plain white and black with a built-up-area pictogram, so it is less distinctive
border: none: blue runs to the edge
innerBorder: white #F6F6F6, ~2.5% of height, inset ~1.5%, rounded. NOT confirmed by a source (low confidence)
lettering: SNV, confirmed by the SNV article and the German Wikipedia comparison of European road signs. The researcher's 'Helvetica Medium Italic for tourist/institution destinations' was not found in any source and has been dropped. Free alternative: Barlow Semi Condensed Medium or Roboto Condensed. White, mixed case
extras: Cities and municipalities are white on blue (F29). Hamlets, industrial estates and institutions are black on white (F33a). Motorway signs are also white on blue; one GeoGuessr guide says signs pointing TO a motorway are green, which was not confirmed in the regulations. Signs are monolingual (Dutch in Flanders, French in Wallonia) and bilingual in Brussels. The blue hex is a RAL 5017 approximation; no official Belgian RAL was found. Correction: the new road code from 1 June 2027 renumbers F1 as R23 (begin), and R25 is the END sign, not F1. Old signs may stay until 2045
wear: Posts, or an overhead gantry on major roads. Rain streaks and grime run down from the top edge. The blue is slightly weathered

signType: Place-name sign F27.1 'Paikannimi' (old no. 662): a blue rectangle with the name in white. The built-up-area sign is a separate one (E22 'Taajama')
border: none: blue runs to the edge
innerBorder: thin white line ~2.5% of height, inset ~1.5%. NOT confirmed (the search ran out before it could be checked)
lettering: Finnish traffic-sign typeface: drawn in the 1960s, prescribed by Traficom, with no published official name. Väylävirasto released it under CC0 as 'Liikennemerkkien kirjasintyyppi (vanha)', and '(vanha)' (old) suggests a newer version exists. Free alternative: 'Tie' (CC0 conversion). Correction: Helsinki (LudwigType) is a COMMERCIAL font inspired by it, not a free alternative. White, mixed case
extras: Blue place-name sign. Places with both Finnish and Swedish names show both, usually on two lines. Ordinary road numbers are on blue, regional road numbers are black on white, and motorway signs are green. The blue hex is an estimate with no source: Finnish rules give colours by chromaticity, and no official hex or RAL was found
wear: Galvanised posts. Road salt and gravel spray along the bottom. Slightly faded blue. Snow or frost on top in winter

signType: Green primary-route direction sign used on main A-roads (white legend, yellow route numbers). Confirmed; it is the most recognisable choice. The white village name sign (white, black border, black Transport Heavy) is the plainer alternative.
bg: #33533B (approx. BS 381C 226 Middle Brunswick Green; roads.org.uk calls primary green equivalent to it; this hex is an unofficial screen value; retroreflective film looks a little brighter)
fg: #FFFFFF legend and arrows. Route numbers are yellow, approx. #FDD906 (BS 381C 355 'Lemon' per roads.org.uk; hex from w3schools). This corrects the earlier #FFCC00.
border: White #FFFFFF at the outer edge, 1.5 stroke widths wide (stroke width = x-height/4, so 3/8 of the x-height). That is about 6-8% of a one-line panel's height. The earlier 4-5% was too thin for a one-line sign.
cornerRadius: Rounded, about 6-8% of a one-line panel's height (no source found for the exact radius)
lettering: Transport Medium (white on dark; Transport Heavy is for dark on light). Real signs use mixed case; capitals are acceptable for the country name. Free close fonts: Transport Medium from roads.org.uk (Nathaniel Porter) or GitHub smugpie/uk-ire-road-sign-fonts. Check each licence before shipping on Google Play.
extras: Yellow route number in brackets, e.g. '(A23)'; a white arrow; a distance figure; stacked panels
wear: Galvanised grey tubular posts and a plain grey back; light road-spray grime along the bottom; grass verge. The game's track (Crystal Palace) is suburban London, so a kerbside pavement mount also fits.

signType: Town-entry sign EB10 (panneau d'entrée d'agglomération): white field, red border, white listel, black capitals. Confirmed. The alternative is the green main-road direction sign with white capitals (L2).
bg: #F6F6F6 (approx. RAL 9016 traffic white; French colours are set by chromaticity, not RAL)
border: Red, approx. RAL 3020 traffic red: #C1121C (w3schools) or #CC0605 (other tables). About 6-8% of the height (no source for the exact width). A thin white listel, about 1.5%, runs outside the red band.
innerBorder: none (the red band is the frame)
cornerRadius: Rounded, about 5-6% of the height (no source for the exact value)
lettering: Caractères L1: upright, bold, black on white, capitals only (confirmed). Free close font: Frank Rausch's 'Caracteres L1' freeware; its licence is custom, so check it before shipping.
extras: Only the place name is allowed on the sign. A second line with the commune name is possible when it differs. 'Village fleuri' and similar notices go on a separate plate above. Exit sign EB20 has a red diagonal bar. In this repo France is used only by the test track Riviera.
wear: Low mount (about 1-1.5 m) on two galvanised posts; clean or slightly dusty; at verges or roundabout flower beds

signType: Blue arrow-pointed direction sign for extra-urban roads. Blue for extra-urban roads and green for motorways is confirmed by DPR 495/1992 art. 78. The town-entry sign 'inizio centro abitato' (white field, black frame, black letters, art. 131) is less distinctive.
bg: #0E518D (approx. RAL 5017 traffic blue per w3schools; other tables give #063971-#005B8C; Italian rules set chromaticity, not RAL)
fg: #FFFFFF (white letters and symbols on blue per art. 78)
border: White #FFFFFF at the edge, about 3-4% of the height (white frames on blue are confirmed; no source for the width)
cornerRadius: Square end on one side; the other end is pointed like an arrow (extra-urban direction blades). Rectangular panels have slightly rounded corners, about 4%.
lettering: Alfabeto Normale (a heavier derivative of Transport); Alfabeto Stretto (condensed) for long names. This corrects the earlier mixed-case claim: per Wikipedia, names are mostly in CAPITALS, with lowercase only sometimes (districts, attractions). Free close font: CCRIGE (Spanish Carretera Convencional, nearly identical to Normale; draft, check licence). No free official version found.
extras: Several pointed blades stacked on one pole; a distance in km. A road number such as 'SS 1' may appear, but its layout was not verified. In this repo Italy is used only by the test track Toskana.
wear: Sun-faded blue film, galvanised poles, sometimes slightly crooked or with stickers; dusty Mediterranean roadside

signType: French EB10-style place sign (white, red border), chosen as a guess. The sources contradict each other: the main Wikipedia microstates article says Monaco uses the Italian design, a Wikipedia draft says the French design, and no official Monegasque source was found. As a city-state Monaco has no town-entry signs of its own. Red-on-white also matches the flag.
border: Red, approx. RAL 3020 (#C1121C to #CC0605), about 6-8% of the height, with a thin white outer listel
lettering: Caractères L1-style capitals (Comparison of European road signs lists Monaco among countries that write destinations in capitals). Free close font: 'Caracteres' freeware (check licence).
extras: Optional smaller second line 'MÙNEGU', the Monégasque name; old-town street signs are bilingual French/Monégasque. No coat of arms or crown, to keep it generic. In this repo Monaco is used only by the test track Monte Carlo, so this sign has low priority.
wear: Very clean and well kept; on painted poles or fixed to a wall or railing in a dense city

signType: Blue advance direction sign 6.9.1 / 6.10.1 outside built-up areas: blue means the route uses an ordinary road, green means a motorway (PDD Appendix 1). Alternatives: town-entry sign 5.23.1 (white, black letters) or 5.25 (blue, white letters).
bg: #1C5AA6 (screen estimate; GOST R 52290 sets colours by chromaticity, no official RAL found)
border: Thin white edge, about 2-3% of the height (seen on real signs; no source for the width)
cornerRadius: Slightly rounded, about 3% of the height (no source found)
lettering: GOST road-sign typeface (from GOST 10807-78, in GOST R 52290-2004, replaced by GOST R 52290-2024). Real place names are usually written with a capital initial and lowercase after (unconfirmed); capitals are acceptable in the game. The earlier 'Arial' claim was dropped as unsupported. Free close font: 'Russian Road Sign' by A. Sapozhnikov (localfonts.eu; Cyrillic and Latin; licence unclear, check it).
extras: Cyrillic name with a Latin line below. Real signs transliterate by GOST R 52290 ('ROSSIYA'), not translate, but the game can show 'РОССИЯ' over 'RUSSIA'. Distance in km at the bottom of 6.9.1; arrows.
wear: Faded film, road-spray or mud streaks on the lower half, grey steel posts. The game's track (Katu-Jaryk, Altai) is a mountain gravel road, so dusty gravel verges fit better than snow.

signType: Green guide (destination) sign on conventional roads and freeways (MUTCD); city-limit signs commonly use the same white-on-green look
bg: #006747 (MUTCD Green; FHWA printing reference Pantone 342, hex as in the Commons table and US heraldic colour list; #006B54 also circulates for Pantone 342; legal spec is chromaticity only, no official hex)
border: White, running to the panel edge (MUTCD 2009 Sec. 2A.14, not 2A.15: a light border on a dark background sits at the edge); about 1-2 in wide, ~0.02-0.04 x height (width not re-verified)
lettering: FHWA Series (Highway Gothic) E(M) for destinations; free alternative Overpass (OFL); Roadgeek 2005 is freeware with an unclear licence. Correction: place names are mixed case on conventional-road guide signs too (MUTCD 2009 2D.05; capitals ~1.33x lower-case loop height), only words like NORTH or EXIT in caps. Correction: Clearview IA-5 was terminated in 2016 but reinstated in March 2018 as an optional, approval-only font; Highway Gothic remains the norm
cornerRadius: Rounded, about 1/8 of the shorter side, max 12 in (TxDOT, FHWA SHS); ~0.12 x height for signs up to 8 ft tall
extras: Plain flat rectangle; optional route-number panel as a plain white shield with black digits (avoid the trademarked Interstate shield); distances in miles
wear: Retroreflective sheeting on aluminium, slightly sun-faded green; galvanised steel posts or I-beams on ordinary roads, grey steel truss gantry over freeways

signType: Green destination (guide) sign as used in Quebec and Ontario (the game's tracks are Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Toronto)
bg: #006747 (approx.; same ASTM green as US sheeting, no official hex). Correction: Quebec's 'pellicule verte de type IV' means retroreflective sheeting Type IV, not a shade of green
border: White, at the panel edge, ~0.03 x height (MUTCD-type; width not confirmed)
lettering: Quebec: Highway Gothic series C, D, E or E(M) (MTQ spec). Ontario: older signs Highway Gothic E(M); MTO now uses Clearview on positive-contrast guide signs (some QEW signs since 2016); BC Clearview since 2006. For these tracks use the Highway Gothic look: Overpass. Destinations mixed case
extras: Key cue vs USA: white maple-leaf Trans-Canada marker on green (Ontario and Quebec place numberless TCH markers beside provincial route markers); distances in km; French-only legends in Quebec, bilingual EN/FR in some Ontario areas (not re-verified)
wear: Galvanised steel posts or overhead steel gantries; winter road salt and grime on the lower edge, slightly faded green

signType: Placa de identificacao de municipio (municipality identification / town-entry sign, Manual Brasileiro de Sinalizacao de Transito Vol. III, indication signs; section number not verified)
bg: #003166 (Munsell 5PB 2/8 from the Vol. III draft; I re-computed it with the Munsell renotation, Illuminant C to D65 sRGB, same result; slightly outside sRGB, red clipped; third-party Hextoral gives #003A65)
border: Blue outer margin (orla externa, same blue as the background), thin, ~0.02 x height (width not confirmed)
innerBorder: White inner frame line (orla interna branca) just inside the blue margin, ~0.02-0.03 x height (width not confirmed)
lettering: Vol. III draft: FHWA Standard Alphabets Serie E(M) or Serie D on rural roads; urban roads may also use Helvetica Medium or Arial. Free alternative Overpass (Highway Gothic look). Letter case not confirmed; caps are fine
extras: White inner frame on deep blue is the key cue; destination signs on rodovias are green, Munsell 10G 3/8 (computed #005643, Hextoral #00583F), with the same white inner frame; Portuguese wording, km
wear: Galvanised steel or treated-wood posts; sun-bleached blue, red-earth dust and streaks on rural highways

signType: Green informative destination sign on conventional (non-concession) paved roads, e.g. Ruta 60 to the Los Libertadores pass (Manual de Senalizacion de Transito, D.S. 78/2012)
bg: #006747 (approx.; no official hex found, the manual's colour table was not reachable)
border: White, at the panel edge, ~0.03 x height (not confirmed in sources)
lettering: Ruta CL (Chile's own sign typeface since 2012, rolled out from a 5-road pilot; many existing signs still Highway Gothic). No confirmed free release: approximate with a humanist sans (Fira Sans or Source Sans 3 SemiBold), or Overpass for the older Highway Gothic look. Informative legends may be caps or mixed case per Spanish spelling (2020 amendment); the older rule required caps
extras: Correction: blue background on concession autopistas and autovias (not 'autorrutas'), green on other paved roads, brown only exceptionally for tourist signs; new signs carry the road's route (rol) number; Spanish, km
wear: Galvanised posts, dusty and sun-faded in the dry Andes; snow and grit marks on high mountain roads

signType: Green direction (guide) sign, AS 1742 / AS 1743, used on rural and main roads incl. freeways
bg: #005A3C (approx.; retroreflective green is defined only by AS/NZS 1906.1 chromaticity; an older AS 1743 text maps non-reflective 'standard green' to AS 2700 G12 Holly Green and 'green' to G13 Emerald; the G12 hex #294332 is an unverified third-party conversion)
border: White, at the panel edge, ~0.03 x height (not re-verified)
lettering: AS 1744 alphabet (Highway Gothic-based), Series E(M) for place and route names (not re-verified; search budget ran out); free alternative Overpass. Place names caps on many rural signs, mixed case on some newer signs
extras: Correction: alphanumeric route marker is gold/yellow characters on a green rectangle (e.g. 'M1', 'A32'); a white border is used only in the ACT, elsewhere the border is gold; distances in km
wear: Galvanised steel posts; sun-faded green, red outback dust on the lower edge

signType: Town-entry sign at the start of a built-up area (E 55, 'tættere bebygget område'; the town-name panel is called a byskilt). Look: white board, black frame, black name, a small town symbol. Confirmed by sources: the meaning of E 55 and of E 56 (its end), and that the byskilt marks where the zone begins. Estimated: colours, frame and lettering. They come from the official sign diagram as I remember it; no page I could read stated them.

signType: Place-name sign (ortnamnsmärke): a blue board with the name in white capitals. Confirmed by Swedish Wikipedia: guide signs on country roads have a blue field with white capital letters, motorways are green, and destinations inside built-up areas are white. Also confirmed: the place-name sign marks a locality and carries no traffic rule. Estimated: that this place-name sign is the blue kind (my reading of those two pages), plus the frame and corner size.
